extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in differential equations / dynamical systems
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria, theorems, and numerical-experiment tasks for studying equilibria, linearization, stability, sinks/sources/saddles, stable/unstable manifolds, and basic numerical integrators (Euler, Improved Euler, Runge–Kutta). Geared toward analyzing local behavior of nonlinear systems and empirically evaluating ODE solvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variational equation / derivative of the flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Dφ_t(X0) U0 = U(t, U0). The derivative of the time-t flow map applied to an initial perturbation U0 equals the solution U(t) of the variational equation along the base solution X(t) with initial value U0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If X(t) is a solution of X' = F(X), the variational equation along X(t) is U' = D F(X(t)) U. Thus ∂φ/∂X applied to U0 is obtained by solving the corresponding variational equation starting at U0. Example: for x' = x^2 explicit calculation verifies this relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearized system at an equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: At an equilibrium X0 the linearized system is U' = D F(X0) U (constant matrix A). Its flow is exp(tA) U0, and near an equilibrium the nonlinear phase portrait 'resembles' that of the linearized system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This local resemblance will be made precise by the Linearization Theorem for hyperbolic equilibria. Beware: resemblance holds under hyperbolicity hypotheses; when the linearization has zero real-part eigenvalues or centers the nonlinear terms can dramatically change behavior (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's method (explicit) for first-order ODEs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate time grid t_{k+1} = t_k + Δt. Small Δt (step size) generally improves accuracy. Used in experiments to approximate solutions (e.g., x' = x with x(0)=1 to approximate e). Also used as a building block for other methods (Improved Euler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improved Euler's method (Heun's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute mk = f(t_k, x_k), y_k = x_k + mk Δt, n_k = f(t_{k+1}, y_k), then x_{k+1} = x_k + (mk + n_k)/2 Δt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the average of two slopes (slope at the beginning and an Euler-predicted slope at the end) to step forward. Recommended in the exploration to compare accuracy vs Euler and Runge–Kutta for various step sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth-order Runge–Kutta method (classical RK4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define m_k = f(t_k, x_k), n_k = f(t_k + Δt/2, x_k + m_k Δt/2), p_k = f(t_k + Δt/2, x_k + n_k Δt/2), q_k = f(t_k + Δt, x_k + p_k Δt), and set x_{k+1} = x_k + (m_k + 2 n_k + 2 p_k + q_k)/6 Δt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General-purpose solver widely used. In exploration tasks it's the method compared against Euler and Improved Euler; students are asked to observe its fourth-order convergence (error decreases rapidly with step size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evaluation metric for numerical methods: error and convergence ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare effectiveness of numerical methods by computing errors at a target time (e.g., x(1)) for multiple step sizes and computing ratios of errors (ρ_{0.1}/ρ_{0.05}, ρ_{0.05}/ρ_{0.01}) to study convergence order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exploration prescribes applying Euler, Improved Euler, and RK4 with Δt = 0.1, 0.05, 0.01 to x' = x (x(0)=1), compute errors vs true value (e = 2.71828182845...), and analyze how errors change under halving or scaling the step size by 1/5. Use spreadsheets for lengthy calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical methods can fail / sensitivity and chaos experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical methods (especially simple ones like Euler) can behave poorly on some problems and exhibit sensitive dependence on initial conditions (chaos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploration: use dy/dt = e^t sin y with initial y(0)=0.3 and compute numerical approximations at t=10 with various Δt (0.3, 0.001, 0.002, 0.003) and slightly perturbed initial conditions (0.301, 0.302) to observe sensitive dependence and breakdown of methods. Check whether RK4 changes behavior relative to Euler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: equilibrium point
rubrics_metrics.description: X* ∈ R^n is an equilibrium point if F(X*) = 0 for the differential equation X' = F(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equilibria can often be written down explicitly by solving algebraic equations, and are central since linearization techniques can be used to study local dynamics when explicit solutions are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: hyperbolic equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: An equilibrium X0 is hyperbolic if all eigenvalues of D F(X0) have nonzero real parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbolicity is the key hypothesis for the Linearization Theorem: local conjugacy to the linearized flow holds when the equilibrium is hyperbolic. Non-hyperbolic cases (zero real part eigenvalues or centers) require further analysis because nonlinear terms may alter behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sink / source criteria (linear and nonlinear)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all eigenvalues of the linearized system at X* have negative real parts then X* is a sink (asymptotically stable). If eigenvalues have positive real parts it's a source (unstable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For planar systems the vector field points into small circles near a sink (dot product negative). The theorem: if all eigenvalues have negative real parts then X* is asymptotically stable. Examples show extension to complex eigenvalues with negative real part and the effect of repeated eigenvalues is addressed by suitable coordinate forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearization Theorem (local conjugacy under hyperbolicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an n-dimensional system X' = F(X) has a hyperbolic equilibrium X0, then the nonlinear flow is conjugate to the flow of the linearized system in a neighborhood of X0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook states the theorem (no proof here) and notes the proof requires analytic techniques when both positive and negative real-part eigenvalues are present. Several examples and constructions (e.g., polar-coordinate conjugacy) illustrate local linearization in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: When linearization fails to determine behavior (non-hyperbolic cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the linearized system has a zero eigenvalue or a center (purely imaginary eigenvalues), adding nonlinear terms often completely changes the phase portrait; linearization may not determine local behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples (e.g., x' = x^2, y' = -y and systems with r' = α r^3, θ' = 1) illustrate that nonlinear terms, however small, can produce qualitatively different dynamics (spiraling toward/away from origin or changing invariant sets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable Curve Theorem (existence and properties of local stable curve for saddle)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a planar system of the form x' = λ x + f1(x,y), y' = -µ y + f2(x,y) with -µ < 0 < λ and f_j(x,y)/r → 0 as r → 0, there exists ε > 0 and a curve x = h_s(y) defined for |y| < ε with h_s(0)=0 such that: (1) solutions starting on the curve remain on it for all t ≥ 0 and tend to the origin as t → ∞; (2) the curve passes through the origin tangent to the y-axis; (3) other solutions in the disk of radius ε leave the disk as t increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The curve x = h_s(y) is the local stable curve W^s_loc(0). Analogous Unstable Curve Theorem gives y = h_u(x) tangent to x-axis. Hypotheses include that f_j are higher-order (quadratic+) so f_j/r → 0. Proof outline and geometric lemmas (cone arguments, reparametrization) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-dimensional stable/unstable manifolds (saddles)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the linearization at an equilibrium has k eigenvalues with negative real parts and n-k with positive real parts, then local stable and unstable sets are k- and (n-k)-dimensional submanifolds respectively; each can be expressed locally as the graph of a C^∞ function g with g(0)=0 and all partial derivatives zero at 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the planar stable/unstable curve result: manifolds are tangent at the equilibrium to the corresponding linear stable/unstable subspaces and intersect only at the equilibrium. Example: conversion to coordinates showing a stable paraboloid in R^3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: stability vs asymptotic stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Stable equilibrium: for every neighborhood O of X* there exists neighborhood O1 ⊂ O so every solution starting in O1 stays in O for all t>0. Asymptotically stable: additionally solutions starting in O1 tend to X* as t → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asymptotic stability is important physically. The text gives the theorem: if all eigenvalues of the linearized system at X* have negative real parts, then X* is asymptotically stable. Examples contrast stable-but-not-asymptotically-stable (center) and unstable equilibria (sources, saddles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallness condition for higher-order terms (hj/r → 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: In local analyses one assumes the higher-order nonlinear terms h_j(x,y) satisfy lim_{(x,y)→(0,0)} h_j(x,y)/r = 0 where r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition formalizes 'higher order' (quadratic or higher) and is used repeatedly in proofs (sink argument, stable curve theorem) to ensure nonlinear terms are negligible compared to linear part near the origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time reparametrization invariance of solution curves (multiplying vector field by positive function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplying the vector field by a smooth positive scalar function does not change solution curves (only their parametrization in time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proofs (stable curve theorem) to simplify sign/monotonicity arguments (e.g., choose g(x,y) positive so y' = -y in a reparametrized system), enabling uniqueness and monotonicity arguments for solution separation.
